posts.title: EU AI Act in 6 swipes
posts.goal: Saves and authority; time-sensitive governance hook
posts.hook: The EU AI Act dates just moved. Here's the version that's current.

slides.headline: The EU AI Act in 6 swipes.
slides.sub: Risk tiers, fines, and the dates that moved.

slides.headline: It sorts AI by risk.
slides.body: Four tiers. Your obligations follow the tier your system falls in.

slides.headline: The four tiers
items: High: risk management, documentation, human oversight, conformity assessment
Limited: transparency. Tell people it's AI

slides.label: of global annual turnover, or €35M
slides.body: Maximum fine for prohibited AI. High-risk violations: up to €15M or 3%.

slides.headline: The dates, as of today
items: Dec 2027: Annex III high-risk (deferred by the Digital Omnibus)

slides.label: 2026 · next date
slides.body: Two new Article 5 prohibitions apply: NCII and CSAM generation.

slides.headline: Who it covers.
slides.body: Anyone placing AI on the EU market or putting it into service in the EU, including non-EU companies serving EU users.

slides.headline: Save this. Full guide on AI Hub.
slides.body: aihubswiss.org/compliance

posts.caption:
The EU AI Act deadlines moved, and a lot of what's still circulating is out of date.

As of today: prohibitions have applied since Feb 2025, general-purpose AI duties since Aug 2025, Article 50 transparency duties since Aug 2026. The Digital Omnibus deferred standalone high-risk (Annex III) obligations to Dec 2027. Next date on the calendar: 2 December 2026.

Swipe for the risk tiers, the fines and who it covers. Save it for your next governance meeting.

General information, not legal advice. Check the Act and your counsel for your situation.

posts.title: Case study: claims triage
posts.goal: Proof post; drive free sign-ins to read full case studies
posts.hook: How one insurer cut claim settlement time by 40%.

slides.headline: How one insurer cut claim settlement time by 40%.
slides.sub: The problem, the build, the numbers.

slides.headline: The problem.
slides.body: 6M+ property and casualty claims a year across 30+ countries. Simple and complex claims waited in the same queue. Average settlement: 17 days.

slides.headline: The build.
slides.body: Language models to sort claims by complexity. Computer vision to assess damage from photos. Rules-based automation for the simple ones.

slides.label: faster settlement
slides.body: From about 17 days to about 10.

slides.label: straight-through
slides.body: Of claims processed with no human touch.

slides.headline: The pattern.
slides.body: Sort by complexity first. Automate the simple. Put people on the hard cases.

slides.headline: 86 case studies. Measured outcomes.
slides.body: Free sign-in unlocks the full write-ups.

posts.caption:
A claim doesn't need an adjuster just because it's a claim.

This AI Hub case study follows an insurer that sorted claims by complexity, assessed damage from photos and straight-through processed the simple ones. Reported results: settlement time down about 40%, with 30% of claims handled with no human touch.

Figures are as reported in the case study entry. The full write-up covers the context, tech stack and lessons.

There are 86 case studies on AI Hub, each with measured outcomes. Free sign-in unlocks them.

Save this if your team is scoping an automation pilot.

posts.title: We published nothing on 31 October
posts.goal: Trust and independence story; shares and follows
posts.hook: We published nothing on 31 October. On purpose.

slides.headline: We published nothing on 31 October. On purpose.
The run.
slides.body: Our daily update searched regulation, models and tools, and funding for 29 to 31 October 2026.

slides.headline: The result.
slides.body: Nothing cleared two independent sources in that window. So nothing was added.

slides.headline: The rule.
slides.body: Two named sources for every claim. Never fabricate.

slides.headline: The caveat.
slides.body: That's not the same as nothing happening. The log says so.

slides.headline: Why it matters.
slides.body: A reference is only useful if you can trust what's on it. A gap beats a guess.

slides.headline: Read the daily update log.
slides.body: Independent. Hand-verified.

posts.caption:
A feed that has to post every day will eventually post something unverified.

On 31 October, our daily update searched regulation, models and tools, and funding, and found nothing dated 29 to 31 October that was backed by two independent sources. So we added nothing, and the log says exactly that.

That's the rule: two named sources for every claim, never fabricate. A gap in a reference is better than a guess.

If you want an AI reference that behaves like this, follow along.
